articles.title: Where machine learning did help: forecasting market volatility
articles.excerpt: Guessing whether a stock goes up next month turned out to be close to impossible in our tests. Guessing how bumpy the market will be is a different problem, and an easier one. Calm periods tend to fol…
articles.body: Guessing whether a stock goes up next month turned out to be close to impossible in our tests. Guessing how bumpy the market will be is a different problem, and an easier one. Why volatility is more predictable Calm periods tend to follow calm periods, and stormy ones follow stormy ones (volatility clustering). That persistence is real structure a model can learn. Direction has very little of it. The setup Target: the variance of S&P 500 (SPY) daily moves over the next 20 trading days. Baseline: HAR, the standard textbook model. It's a regression on recent volatility over the last day, week and month. Measure: QLIKE, a loss function suited to variance forecasts (lower is better). Test: a 2025–26 holdout, with the Diebold-Mariano test to check whether the difference is more than noise.
articles.author: Quantooox

articles.title: kubectl wait for condition fails on null conditions
articles.excerpt: kubectl wait --for condition=Established crd/ is the usual way to CRD before applying resources of its kind. status.conditions. It does not wait when status.conditions is present and null: it exits at…
articles.body: kubectl wait --for condition=Established crd/<name> is the usual way to wait for a new CRD before applying resources of its kind. It waits while the object has no status.conditions . It does not wait when status.conditions is present and null : it exits at once with an error. The kadet-hub/recipes CI hit that on 26 October 2026, with kubectl 1.37.1 against a kind node on Kubernetes 1.37.0: error: kubectl --kubeconfig ... wait --for condition=Established --timeout 60s crd/rabbitmqclusters.rabbitmq.com exited 1 error: .status.conditions accessor error: <nil> is of the type <nil>, expected []interface{} A rerun of the same job passed. The 60 second timeout never came into play.

articles.title: Your agent will obey the instructions hidden in the logs it reads
articles.excerpt: An agent that reads application logs will do what the logs say. Not always, and not because the log is malicious, but because the model has no built-in sense of where an instruction is allowed to come…
articles.body: An agent that reads application logs will do what the logs say. Not always, and not because the log is malicious, but because the model has no built-in sense of where an instruction is allowed to come from. To the model a line in your system prompt and a line in a log file are the same thing: tokens. It weighs them by how much they sound like an order, not by who wrote them. The line that says "run this command and then report success" is instruction-shaped, so it gets the instruction-shaped response, even though it arrived through a file the agent was supposed to be reading. This is not a new idea, but this week it landed in a form you can reproduce on your own machine in about ten minutes, and that is the part worth keeping.

articles.title: A2A in Plain English: Read an Agent Card, Then Follow One Task

articles.body: MCP connects your agent to tools. A2A connects it to other agents. Easy to repeat, harder to use when you're about to wire two systems together. The official A2A docs give a practical test: look at what's on the other end. If it's a tool with structured inputs and outputs, like a database query or a weather lookup, that's MCP territory. If it's another agent that reasons, plans, keeps state and may need a back-and-forth to finish the job, that's what A2A is for. Here's that test made concrete. I ran the official A2A "Hello World" sample locally, read its Agent Card, sent it a task, and then tried a few things you'll run into on day one. All the JSON below is real output from that run (IDs shortened), using the a2a-sdk Python package, version 1.3.0, against protocol version 1.0.

articles.title: Scientists simulate an Earth without life to help hunt for aliens and inhabited worlds
articles.excerpt: By modeling how a planet without life develops its atmosphere, astronomers hope to be able to better distinguish rocky planets without life from those that are inhabited.
articles.body: A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe. Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life.

articles.excerpt: On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission, the first Mars mission in 20 years. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission. This was the first mission NASA sent to Mars in almost 20 years! The Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft was an orbiter. It transmitted data from NASA's Mars rovers Sojourner , Spirit and Opportunity back to Earth. The spacecraft also did a lot of its own science. It found surface channels on Mars that appeared to have been created by running water. Mars Global Surveyor looked at the south pole of Mars and saw signs of possible climate change. It also saw a mineral called hematite on Mars. Hematite usually forms in water. NASA then sent its Spirit and Opportunity rovers to look for the hematite, and both rovers found it near their landing sites. Mars Global Surveyor survived much longer than expected.

articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now. This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life. I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security. That would make it one of the world's most valuable companies, not long after raising $122 billion from investors in March at a valuation of $852 billion. Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion.
